list.listitem: Use the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) diagnostic criteria () to determine whether rheumatoid arthritis is present and the Netherlands RA Clinical Prediction Score to estimate the probability of developing rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in 1 year. C
Because joint destruction in RA begins within a few weeks of symptom onset, early diagnosis and treatment with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) is vital. B
Patients at risk of developing persistent or erosive arthritis should be started on DMARDs as soon as possible, even if they do not yet fulfill all established classification criteria. B
Among the DMARDs, methotrexate is considered to be the anchor drug and should be used first in patients at risk of developing persistent disease. B
Patients with an inadequate response to methotrexate alone should be given the combination of methotrexate and a biologic agent. A

background.definition: RA is a chronic systemic, inflammatory disease with autoimmune features characterized by symmetric polyarticular joint swelling, joint pain and destruction, as well as morning stiffness, fatigue, fever, and multiple comorbidities.

list.listitem: Annual RA incidence was 40.9 per 100,000 population (≥18 years).
Females: 53.1 /100,000/year Males: 27.7/100,000/year.
Prevalence of RA is 0.41% to 0.54 %. Female-to-male ratio approximately 3 to 1.
Peak age of onset of RA is 40 to 50 years.

RA is a leading cause of disability and healthcare costs in the US. RA results in increased morbidity and mortality. Currently, drug costs make up most of the direct cost due mainly to the increasing use of biologic agents while inpatient cost of care is decreasing. Indirect costs from absenteeism and work disability account for 39% to 86% of total costs. RA that is inadequately treated results incomplications such as malialigned joints in 80% of patients and inability to work within 10 years from disease onset in 40% of patients .
RA is the most common systemic inflammatory arthritis seen in the primary care setting.
Increased work disability, income reduction, need for extra rest time during the daytime, dramatic changes in leisure activities, reduced transport mobility, and social dependency may occur.
Unknown, however, both environmental and genetic factors appear to play a role.
Theories involving infectious agents have been proposed but none have been clearly established.
Organisms implicated include Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, proteus species, and Escherichia coli with mechanisms remaining elusive and molecular mimicry being postulated.
Genetics: concordance of RA was found to be 9.1% among monozygotic twins and 6.4% among dizygotic twins.
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-linked genes account for 1/3 to 1/2 of genetic susceptibility.
There is an association between human leukocyte antigen (HLA)–DRB1 locus and patients who are positive for rheumatoid factor.
RA is characterized by synovial inflammation and hyperplasia, autoantibody production and systemic features. Both adaptive and innate immune pathways play an integral role in the pathogenesis of RA.
Currently it is felt that unique HLA alleles aid in the development of a specific arthrogenic peptide(s) that activates CD4+ helper T-cells and/or synovial macrophages.

This ultimately leads to the production of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor [TNF]), which then stimulate synovial fibroblast proliferation and production of inflammatory mediators (eg, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and proteolytic enzymes) that destroy cartilage and bone.
The diagnosis of RA is based on joint involvement, autoantibody serology, acute phase reactant and duration of symptoms. C
Determine the duration and extent of morning stiffness; number, distribution, and symmetry of tender and swollen joints; and presence of rheumatoid nodules. C
Clinical examination is the preferred method for detecting synovitis. In doubtful cases, ultrasound or MRI may be considered. B
If the patient has a score of 6 points or more using the ACR criteria (), a diagnosis of RA can be made. C
If 3 or fewer of the 7 ACR criteria are present with persistent joint pain, use the Netherlands RA Clinical Prediction Score to determine probability of patient developing RA in 1 year. C
Order rheumatoid factor (RF), CRP level, ESR level, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP), and hand and wrist radiographs to look for erosions or periarticular osteopenia. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Acute onset, mostly males, formation of tophi
No persistent small joint synovitis, involvement of proximal muscles of shoulder and pelvis
Abdominal complaints, involves weight bearing joints
Noninflammatory distal interphalangeal, proximal interphalangeal (PIP), weight-bearing joints

list.listitem: Older diagnostic criteria for RA are shown in .

No formal diagnostic criteria currently exist for RA but the American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) 2010 classification criteria can aid in diagnosis of RA. ACR/EULAR 2010 classification criteria require that at least 1 joint has definite clinical synovitis not explained by another disease plus 1 of the following: a) presence of long-standing disease previously satisfying classification criteriab) presence of ≥ 2 typical periarticular erosionsc) a score of 6 points or more using the ACR criteria (Table 1).
The criteria are very sensitive for moderate or advanced RA but ineffective for diagnosing early RA.

Patients with inflammatory arthritis not meeting the ACR criteria have undifferentiated arthritis. The Netherlands RA Clinical Prediction Score, consisting of various clinical features and laboratory values, can identify the likelihood of meeting the ACR criteria for RA in the following year.

Suspect RA in patients with painful swollen hands for at least 3 weeks involving metacarpophalangeals (MCPs), PIPs, and wrist joints, and accompanied by morning stiffness usually lasting more than 1 hour. The distal interphalangial joints and lumbar spine are not usually involved in patients with RA.
Systemic symptoms emerge over weeks to months and commonly include anorexia, weakness, fatigue, malaise, and low-grade fever.

In 300 consecutive patients fulfilling the ACR criteria for RA, the onset was rapid in 46%. Initial involvement occurred in small joints in 31%, medium joints in 16%, large joints in 28%, and combined sites in 25%. The pattern of joint involvement at onset was monoarticular in 21%, pauciarticular in 44%, and polyarticular in 35%.
About 20% of patients with early RA report no morning stiffness, whereas nearly half report stiffness for at least 1 hour.
Compared with MRI, clinical evaluation of the hands and wrists of patients with RA was only 43% sensitive and 89% specific for detecting synovitis.
Because of its prognostic role, all patients with RA should be evaluated for the number of swollen and tender joints.

Extra-articular manifestation in RA is present in 8% to 40% of patients and include the following: a. Cardiac: accelerated atherosclerosis and pericarditis b. Eye: episcleritis, scleritis, keratoconjunctivitis sicca and peripheral ulcerative keratitis. c. Hematologic: amyloidosis and Felty syndrome (splenomegaly, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia) d. Nervous system: cervical myelopathy and neuropathy e. Pulmonary: Caplan syndrome (Nodules and pneumoconiosis), interstitial lung disease, pleural effusion and pulmonary nodules f. Skin: rheumatoid nodules and vasculitis
Most patients with RA will exhibit systemic inflammation, indicated by elevations in sedimentation rate, CRP, RF, and anti-CCP antibodies.

Because joint erosions can occur rapidly and their presence is one component of the American Rheumatism Association diagnostic criteria, radiographs of both hands and wrists should be performed on any patient suspected to have RA. The radioscaphoid and radiolunate joints are the earliest and have the most severe radiographic progression in patients with RA. Scaphoid erosions often were seen early in about 1/4 of patients. Other radiograph findings include joint space narrowing, soft tissue swelling, cysts, cartilage loss and cortical thinning. Radiograph of the neck in flexion can be used to investigate odontoid ligament laxity with symptoms including neck pain, sensory loss and quadriparesis.
In patients with longer duration of disease, about 3/4 have distal radioulnar joint involvement.
In primary care patients with RA and patients with seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis, the rate of symmetric erosions on hand and wrist radiographs is about the same (about 60%).

In 22 patients with RA, ultrasound of the knee detected effusions in about 61% of the knees compared with clinical examination, which only detected 36%. Ultrasound was very accurate for detection of erosions and moderately accurate for detection of synovitis in a study of 40 patients with RA and 20 healthy controls. Plain radiography was very specific and helpful when abnormal, but lacked sensitivity.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation, and for a suggested approach to treatment.
A validated risk score can predict the likelihood of rheumatoid arthritis one year later, based on physical findings and laboratory tests.

Early diagnosis and treatment with disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are vital; patients at risk of developing persistent or erosive arthritis should be started with DMARDs even if they do not yet meet all of the established classification criteria. B
Among the DMARDS, methotrexate is considered to be the anchor drug, and should be used first in patients at risk of developing persistent disease. B
NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroid injections, and low-dose oral corticosteroids provide short-term relief of symptoms. A

Nonbiologic DMARDs (hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and leflunomide) and biologic response modifiers (tumor necrosis factor inhibitors like etanercept, infliximab, and adalimumab) retard the progression of joint erosion and are most beneficial when used early. A

Methotrexate is the recommended initial DMARD. For patients with an inadequate response to methotrexate alone, ACR guidelines (2021) recommend addition of a biologic DMARD over triple therapy with methotrexate, hydrochloroquine and sulfasalazine. B

Although patients with RA have a higher risk for CVD and CVD mortality than the general population, primary prevention with atorvastatin did not improve CV outcomes over placebo in an underpowered randomized trial. B

Management goals include using a multidisciplinary approach to minimize pain and inflammation and preserve joint, physical, social, and emotional functions; quality of life; capacity to work; and control systemic complications. C

They are multiple classes of drugs used to manage patients with RA. These include disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti- inflammatory drugs. DMARDs can be further classify into nonbiologic DMARDs and biologic DMARDs.

See for an overall approach to managing patients with RA. Patients with mild disease may be started on a nonbiologic such as methotrexate, whereas patients with more severe disease may benefit from a biologic agent or combination of biologic and methotrexate. In spite of all the existing research, there is little data comparing the various DMARDs.

A regimen of methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine ("triple therapy") is a much more cost-effective option for adults with RA and has similar efficacy to newer biologic agents. In a randomized trial with 353 patients with active RA despite an initial course of methotrexate alone, triple therapy was non-inferior to etanercept plus methotrexate.

A randomized, multicenter trial of 200 patients with RA in clinical remission found that a MRI-guided treatment strategy based on bone marrow edema was no better than a traditional treat-to-target strategy in preventing radiographic progression or disease activity after 24 months.

The 2021 guidelines from the American College of Rheumatology recommend methotrexate monotherapy over other non-biologic DMARDs. Agents like hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, and leflunomide are options for DMARD naive patients with low disease activity.

In 2 systematic reviews of RCTs, early treatment with methotrexate was associated with greater treatment response and improved function. Over 50% of patients treated within 1 year of diagnosis responded compared with 43% treated 1 to 2 years after diagnosis, 44% for 2 to 5 years, 38% for 5 to 10 years, and 35% for more than 10 years.
A systematic review of 19 trials comparing treatment with methotrexate alone to a combination of methotrexate and a non-biologic DMARD showed no significant advantage for combination therapy.

In a cohort study of over 2000 patients with RA, about 600 were treated with methotrexate. The risk of death from any cause in patients treated with methotrexate was less than half that of other patients and the cardiovascular death rate was 1/3 that of the other patients.Methotrexate can cause oral and GI problems. Folic acid and folinic acid supplements reduce the frequency of these side effects. The anti-TNF agents show no benefit over methotrexate with regard to clinical outcomes, although they may be more likely to prevent radiographic progression in patients with early RA (NNT 8).

Leflunomide can be used instead of methotrexate in combination with other nonbiologic DMARDs or biologic DMARDs if the patient has side effects with the use of methotrexate. However, leflunomide but does not produce the same clinical improvement compared to methotrexate. Side effects include diarrhea, reversible alopecia, hypertension and dizziness.
In 4 trials with almost 600 patients, those taking hydroxychloroquine had greater improvement in symptom scores and sedimentation rate than patients taking placebo.
Adverse effects included retinopathy, rashes, nightmares, blood disorders, convulsion and depression.

In 6 trials with 468 patients, those taking sulfasalazine had greater improvement in symptom scores and sedimentation rate than patients taking placebo. Side effects include of sulfasalazine includes anorexia, headache, nausea, vomiting, gastric distress, skin rash, fever and anemia.

Only a few small trials have compared acetaminophen with NSAIDs. Although it is unclear which is more effective, patients preferred NSAIDs (NNT 5; 95% CI, 3-13). Celecoxib has a reduced rate of GI complications than naproxen, diclofenac, or ibuprofen after 6 months of therapy, but this benefit may not persist long-erm. Weak oral opioids improve pain scores, but their limited benefits may be offset by a high frequency of adverse effects.

Compared with placebo, patients treated with low-dose steroids (10 mg prednisone daily) experience initial symptomatic improvement, but after 6 months, only grip strength and tenderness scores remain improved. Additionally, there was less radiographic progression after 6 months.

Available data are scant, but seem to provide evidence that low-dose glucocorticoids (10 mg or less of prednisolone or prednisone equivalent) in the treatment of RA do not increase osteoporotic fractures, blood pressure, cardiovascular diseases, or peptic ulcer incidence.
In patients with newly diagnosed RA, minocycline, 100 mg twice daily, had significantly greater reduction in RA activity than patients treated with hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily (NNT 4).

Biologic DMARDs have shown up to a 70% improvement in patients who have failed other therapies. Biologic DMARDs can be further grouped into TNF-alpha blockers, Janus kinase inhibitors, B and T cell-targeted agents and interleukin Inhibitors. They are two types of TNF- alpha blocker- (1) receptor blocker (etanercept) and (2) monoclonal antibody (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab and certilizumab). B and T Cell-Targeted Agents include rituximab and abatacept. Interleukin inhibitors include anakinra and tocilizumab.
A meta-analysis of published RCTs concluded that biologic DMARDs were superior to non-biologics in improving functional outcomes.

A network meta-analysis of studies of 9 biologic DMARDs found statistically significant increases in serious infections (OR 1.37; NNTH 108), TB reactivation (OR 4.68; NNTH 168), and total adverse events.

ACR guidelines (2021) recommend against TNF inhibitors for patients with heart failure, and suggest preferential use of rituximab for patients with another indication such as lymphoproliferative disorder. Corticosteroids are recommended over biologic DMARDs for patients with a serious infection in the previous year. For patients not responding to a biologic DMARD, switching to a biologic DMARD in a different category is recommended.

Etanercept is a TNF-alpha receptor blocker. In 9 RCTs, patients taking etanercept (25 mg twice weekly) had more meaningful reductions in various rheumatologic scores than control patients (NNT ranged from 2 to 7) and slowed joint destruction. Etanercept was found to decrease the rate of new erosion formation. For patients with active RA, weekly injections of 50 mg of etanercept appear as effective as 25 mg twice weekly in improving symptoms. If the patient does not improve with single injections, switch to twice weekly.
A study of 1024 patients switched to a biosimilar version of etanercept found similar benefits to those remaining on the original drug.

Infliximab is a TNF inhibitor. In 2 trials with 529 patients, infliximab (various doses) was better than placebo in improving RA disease activity (NNT ranged from 3 to 13).Adverse effects include nausea, headache, sinusitis and rash.

Certolizumab pegol is a monoclonal antibody that is a TNF-alpha inhibitor. In 5 trials with 2394 patients, certolizumab pegol (50-400 mg daily) was more effective than methotrexate or placebo at improving RA disease activity at 24 and 52 weeks. Adverse effects included hypertension, upper respiratory infection, and nasopharyngitis.

Adalimumab is a monoclonal antibody that is a TNF-alpha inhibitor. In a systematic review of 6 RCTs with almost 2400 patients, adalimumab 40 mg every other week was more effective than placebo in causing meaningful reductions in various rheumatologic scores (NNT ranged from 3 to 38). In one study, there was a higher risk of serious infections in patients taking adalimumab (NNTH 31). This same systematic review also looked at adalimumab combined with methotrexate (or other DMARDs) versus placebo combined with methotrexate (or other DMARDs). Patients receiving adalimumab in combination with other drugs had more meaningful reductions in various rheumatologic scores (NNT ranged from 2 to 13) and slowed joint destruction.Side effects include respiratory infections.

A Cochrane review concluded that fixed-dose down-titration of TNF-alpha inhibitors, specifically etanercept and adalimumab, after low disease activity for 3 to 12 months, is as effective as maintaining the standard dose for outcomes such as disease activity, patient function, and, probably, disease remission. Additionally, disease activity-guided lowering of dose appears as effective as maintaining the standard dose in terms of disease remission and, probably, disease activity.

Baricitinib is a JAK inhibitor. In an RCT of 1307 patients with RA and an inadequate response to methotrexate, at one year those randomized to baricitinib had a greater improvement in standardized disease scores than those randomized to either placebo or adalimumab. Serious adverse events were uncommon, occurring in 5% of patients receiving baricitinib and 2% receiving adalimumab.

Upadacitinib is an oral JAK inhibitor that was compared with abatacept (a T-cell targeting drug) in a randomized trial of 612 patients with RA refractory to biologic DMARDs. More patients in the upadacitinib group achieved remission (30% vs 13%, p < 0.001, NNT = 6). Four patients experienced life-threatening adverse events in the upadacitinib group (1 death, 2 venous thromboemboli, and 1 stroke) so more study is needed to determine whether safety is adequate.

Tofacitinib is a JAK inhibitor approved for treatment of RA. It was associated with increases in lipids and with cancer in early trials. An FDA mandated safety trial randomized 4362 patients 50 and older on methotrexate who had at least one cardiovascular risk factor to tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily, tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily, or a TNF inhibitor. After a median follow-up of 4 years, tofacitinib was associated with both more major adverse cardiovascular events (3.4% vs 2.5%) and a higher incidence of cancer (4.2% vs. 2.9%). Opportunistic infections, non-melanoma skin cancer, and herpes zoster were also more common with tofacitinib.

listitem.em: B and T cell targeting agents

list.listitem: Rituximab is used as a second line therapy in patients with resistant RA after the failure of methotrexate or an anti-TNF therapy.

Abatacept is used to treat patients with moderate to severe RA who were found to have an inadequate response with other nonbiologic DMARDs or biologic DMARDs. Adverse effects includes hypersensitivity reaction and risk of opportunistic infection.
Tocilizumab is an interleukin (IL)-6 inhibitor. In 8 trials with 3334 participants, tocilizumab was 4 times as likely as placebo to lead to RA disease remission, but increased cholesterol levels.

Anakinra is an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. In a Cochrane review of 5 trials, anakinra (50-150 mg daily) was more effective than placebo in various rheumatologic and pain scores; injection site reactions were significantly higher than placebo (71% vs 28%, respectively).

Many patients developing severe joint destruction and loss of function undergo surgery to improve function; however, rigorous data are limited. Since 1998, the rate of orthopedic surgery in patients with RA declined, perhaps related to better medical therapy.

In 5 trials with 346 patients, intra-articular steroid injections caused greater improvements in morning stiffness, swelling, pain scores, and range of motion compared to patients receiving placebo injections.

RA hand surgery includes both prophylactic and reconstructive procedures. Prophylactic procedures delay the destructive RA processes and includes tenosynovectomy, joint synovectomy, and tendon rebalancing. Reconstructive procedures include arthrodesis, arthroplasty and tendon transfer.
After about 14 years of follow-up, only 1/3 of patients treated with silicone metacarpophalangeal arthroplasty expressed satisfaction and only 1/4 were pain free.

In a trial of 67 patients with RA not responding to intensive medical therapy treated with radical multiple synovectomy, after 3 years of follow-up patients treated surgically had reductions in swollen and tender joints as well as lower sedimentation rates and CRPs than control patients. More than 40% of the patients remained in clinical remission.

2017 ACR/AAHKS guidelines made the following recommendations regarding perioperative management of antirheumatic medications in patients undergoing total hip or knee arthroplasty: (1) DMARDs: continue methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide, and doxycycline; (2) Biologics/monoclonal antibodies: stop medications prior to surgery and schedule surgery at the end of the usual dosing cycle, relative to the last dose, then restart no sooner than 2 weeks after surgery assumin good healing and no infection.
The evidence for acupuncture and electroacupuncture in treating patients with RA is poor and inconclusive.
In a systematic review of 7 RCTs with 345 patients, Tai Chi had no effect (good or bad) on disease activity, function, or adverse events.
A systematic review of 22 trials found some evidence that herbal therapies affect RA symptoms, but most trials had research design flaws and inadequate reporting.

Most studies of occupational therapy are of poor quality. In the few high quality studies, there is clear evidence of improvement in functional scores in patients receiving occupational therapy and splints than control patients.
Exercise is of limited benefit, although strengthening may be helpful.
For RA of the hands, a Cochrane review concluded that exercise has either uncertain or only modest efficacy in terms of hand function or pain in the short, medium, and long term.

The data on therapeutic ultrasound is limited to 2 trials with only 80 patients. The methodologic quality combined with the limited data makes it difficult to know whether therapeutic ultrasound is effective. It appears to be more helpful for pain than function.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation and low level laser light therapy are helpful for pain relief in the short term, but not for other outcomes.

In 6 trials with 355 patients, the effectiveness of balneotherapy (spa treatments) could not be established because of poor reporting and poor methods. Most studies, however, reported positive findings.
In 7 small studies with 328 patients, superficial moist heat and paraffin baths provided temporary pain relief.
Diets including Mediterranean, vegetarian and anti-inflammatory have been shown to be modestly beneficial.

Tobacco cessation and limited alcohol consumption are recommended. Smoking is associated with higher RA disease activity and severity, radiographic progression, and poorer treatment response; the negative impact of high alcohol consumption on these outcomes is less clear.

RA is a chronic disabling disorder that if not treated early can lead to permanent joint destruction and increased risk for developing several comorbidities (eg, cardiovascular disease, lymphoma, and shortened lifespan). B

The following factors predict persistent and erosive disease: number of swollen and tender joints, elevated ESR or CRP, levels of rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, and radiographic erosions. B
Most patients present with an insidious onset that affects small joints of the hands (MCP, PIP) and feet (metatarsophalangeal) before involving larger joints.
Over the years, articular deformities and functional impairment occur commonly. Some patients experience flares and remissions, whereas others a progressive course.
Patients with RA are 7 times more likely to develop greater than moderate disability when compared with age- or sex-matched individuals.
Approximately 50% of patients with RA are unable to work full-time in 10 years.
Life expectancy of patients with RA is decreased by 5 to 10 years.
Other complications include effects on work and social life, restricted mobility, inability to work, depression, vasculitis, cardiovascular reserve, neuropathy, anemia, and lymphatic cancer.

Favorable RA prognosis is characterized by remission, age less than 40 years, acute onset in primarily large joints, disease duration less than 1 year, and negative rheumatoid factor particularly after 1 year.

Unfavorable RA prognosis is associated with a rapid onset in combination with weight loss, fatigue, low-grade fever, rapid appearance of rheumatoid nodules, high levels of rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, persistent polyarticular synovitis, persistent elevated acute phase reactants (CRP, ESR), early radiographic joint damage, lower socio-economic status and education level, presence of major histocompatibility markers and extra-articular disease (cardiovascular disease, lymphoma), presence of HLA-DR4 haplotype.
The Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ), a functional assessment tool, is the most accurate predictor of mortality (1 standard deviation in HAQ score = odds ratio for mortality of 2.3).

Cardiovascular disease in patients with RA is 2 to 4 times higher, occurs 10 years earlier and is not explained by traditional risk factors, and may be secondary to inflammation.However, RA-specific cardiovascular disease risk calculators are no better at predicting risk than traditional risk calculators such as the ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations.
Patients with RA are at an increased risk (2- to 3-fold) for developing lymphoma.
Treatment with biologic therapies do not increase the risk of cancer.
A Danish nationwide matched cohort study found excess mortality in women (but not men) with RA.
Patients who do not achieve remission should be evaluated every 1 to 3 months.
Disease activity monitoring should include counts of tender and swollen joints, sedimentation rate, CRP, as well as global assessments by the patient and the physician.

RA disease activity can be evaluated using scoring systems which include the clinical disease activity index (CDAI) and the simplified disease activity index (SDAI). These scoring systems, primarily the CDAI can be used to follow therapy using the “treat-to-target” approach.
See chapter on juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.
